chapters.title: Scene 1 - Head of the Household
chapters.content:
One summer—or maybe autumn—after the market had ended,
in that hour when the day's dust settles with the sunlight,
the village elders carried our house's wooden porch
and set it down in front of Dongnyeon's house.

As always, a janggi board was laid out on one side,
and the women sat together on the other, talking.

No one remembered how it started,
but the women soon went inside
and came back out with a frying pan, flour, a ladle, cooking oil,
garlic chives, green onions, and a portable gas range.

They mixed the white flour with water into a thick batter.

The pan went on the flame.
Oil shimmered, then bubbled.

A ladleful poured in—

chiiiiii—

An unnamed pancake began to cook.

I was playing janggi with the adults
when a girl from my class, Yongju, said he wanted some jelly.

I suddenly felt like teasing him.

"Yongju! I'll give you some. Hold out your hand."

She did.

"If it's something precious,
you should receive it properly—with both hands."

So She brought both hands together.

"You didn't wash them, did you?
Then it won't taste good. Open your mouth instead."

The fool stepped closer.

"Aaaaaah—"

I dropped something black and soft into her mouth.

She chewed.

Then—

"Hey, you jerk! Isn't this a booger?!"

And She burst into tears.

The adults, who had been watching from the side, burst out laughing.

I said,

"Do you usually eat boogers?
How else would you know so fast?"

Yongju's father laughed the loudest.

"Dong-gi's right!
Looks like our Yongju eats them all the time!"

Yongju, embarrassed, stopped crying soon enough.

Her father suddenly lifted me onto her shoulders
and walked around the neighborhood, shouting,

"Dong-gi is this village's treasure!
When the grown-ups get bored,
he's the one who makes things interesting!"

That felt strange.

Usually, my mother—or someone—would've scolded me.

But that day, everyone only smiled.

He set me down.

"Dong-gi.
You should keep getting along with Yongju."

He held out her little finger.

I hooked mine around it
and sealed the promise.

A few months later,
I heard that Yongju's father had died of cancer.

After that, their family gave up the business.
The door of "Yongju-Kokne Hair Salon" never opened again.

The alley between their house and Dongnyeon's—
the one we used to take to Pine Tree Garden—
was blocked by a large gate.

The wall grew higher.

After that,
whenever I saw Yongju,
that moment came back to me.

So I never spoke to her again.
Never teased her.

Until I graduated middle school
and left for Seoul,

I don't remember
ever having another conversation with her.

At the market, around that time,
several households lost their fathers.

Their doors closed.

They became cut off from the village.

It was then, vaguely,
that I began to understand—

when the head of a household dies,
life becomes harder.

And in Eunpunggol,
his absence
meant poverty.

chapters.title: Scene 2 - Once Upon a Time on the Radio
chapters.content:
DJ:

Alright—
our next letter.

Before I begin,
I should say this.

The producers were laughing...
and then suddenly very quiet.

It's a Lunar New Year story.

From Northern Europe.

The sender—

Huldra.

LETTER

Hello.

My name is Huldra.
I come from the far North—
from Odin's lands.

When I first came to Korea,
I thought winter would be easier.

It's farther south, after all.

DJ:

That assumption...
never ends well.

LETTER

In my homeland,
temperatures fall much lower.

But Korea—

is different.

Minus fifteen degrees,
and the moment you step outside—

the wind hits you
like a knife.

For a second,
you forget how to breathe.

DJ:

In Korea,
winter isn't about numbers.

It's about the wind.

LETTER

That winter,
I survived by washing
only my hands and face.

Then one day—

Ms. M said,

"No matter how cold it is,
you must welcome the New Year clean."

"Let's go to the bathhouse."

DJ:

That's not a suggestion.

That's a command.

LETTER

At the bathhouse—

even ghosts were there.

Men over fifteen
weren't allowed inside.

So we left her son outside
and went in.

People didn't just wash and leave.

They soaked.

Ten minutes.
Twenty.

Then sat down—

and scrubbed
their skin

with towels
like sandpaper.

Ms. M finished first.

Then she turned—
toward me.

DJ:

Uh-oh.

LETTER

She started scrubbing me.

I said it hurt.

I told her to stop.

She didn't.

Then I saw it.

Dark flakes
rolling off my skin.

Falling everywhere.

I felt ashamed.

Was I really this dirty?

But the other women—

even the ghosts—

smiled.

"We all live like that."

"Nothing to be embarrassed about."

DJ (quietly):

...that line stays.

LETTER

Then—

it happened.

Ms. M was showering.

Suddenly—

BOOM.

The wall collapsed.

Completely.

Everyone froze.

Then screamed.

We grabbed towels
and ran—

like dodging a bomb.

DJ:

Wait...
this is a New Year story??

LETTER

They covered the hole
with a tarp.

We got dressed.

Then we heard what happened.

Her son—

outside—

had tried to peek.

Knocked over fertilizer.

The sack hit the wall.

The wall gave way.

Her husband came running.

Apologized.

Paid for everything.

The women laughed.

"Kids will be kids."

And that was it.

DJ:

Up to here...
it's funny.

LETTER

At home,

the father scolded the boy.

Too ashamed
to face the neighborhood.

Ms. M said nothing.

Because—

when the wall collapsed—

she had hit her head.

And still,
she walked around calmly
for days.

DJ:

Wait.

The victim is the mother??

LETTER

Since coming to Korea—

this was the strangest
Lunar New Year
of my life.

But I still remember—

the warmth after,

clean skin,

and banana milk.

I hope
she recovered well.

And someday—

I hope we return
to that bathhouse together.

Thank you.

DJ (closing):

It starts funny.

...and honestly—

it stays funny.

Back then,
most houses didn't even have showers.

So on New Year's,
everyone went to the public bathhouse.

And things like this?

They happened
more often than you'd think.

Thank you, Huldra.

We'll send you a small gift.

Now—
let's listen to a song.

After Listening to the Radio

The story stayed light.

So—

I could joke about it too.

I called Agent M.


"Dokkaebi—
what is he doing these days?"

"He's learning to cook."

"Preparing for MCGW."

"Good."

"The turtle fleets need chefs."

"He's preparing
for his children."

"He's changed a lot."

"He's going to be a father."

"Excellent."

"There are ghosts
in Odin's kingdom
who want to come here."

"Set conditions."

"First—"

"They must be able
to get along
with Korean ghosts
and humans."

"Communication comes first."

"Yes, sir."

"Good."

"Time's up."

"Bye."

I watched her leave.

"Hey—
your boy
is still just a boy."

"Yes, sir."

She ran off
like the wind.

chapters.title: Scene 3 - Two Faces of the Wash-Place
chapters.content:
About thirty meters
from the wash-place,

there was a place
where water was held back.

A sluice gate.

Like a small dam.

People called it—

Cheondangbo.

During farming season,

when water ran short,

it mattered.

Water was drawn from there
into the fields.

It was a little over
two meters deep.

Kids who could swim well
played there sometimes.

One hot summer day—

on the way home
from school—

suddenly,

Byeongha's father
stepped into the water.

He was searching
for something.

And then—

a girl

none of us had ever seen

was pulled out.

We thought—

someone must have fallen in.

Someone pulled her out.

And we went home.

By evening,

we went back
to the riverside.

People were gathered.

Murmuring.

There was something—

covered
with straw bundles
and rice sacks.

The adults sat around it.

No one spoke.

When children tried to look—

someone shouted.

No one in particular.

"Hey!
Get back!"

"This is no place
for children."

The next day at school—

they said someone had drowned.

Teachers spoke all day
about water safety.

"Warm up first."

"Don't jump in."

"Don't go deeper
than your knees."

I just thought—

another accident.

A few days later—

a man came,

carrying bundles
of eggs.

Seonju and I
couldn't even hold them.

So we just stood there—

watching.

"Ma'am... thank you.
Truly... thank you."

"If it hadn't been for you—
we wouldn't have even seen
our youngest one
one last time."

"You're the one
who should be resting."

"And yet you came."

"We kept everyone away.
No one was allowed near."

"But when you shouted—
they moved."

"You said—"

'Shouldn't a father
at least see his daughter's face
on her final journey?'

"And you opened it."

"That's how—
we held her
one last time."

"I will never forget this."

Mother looked at him.

"Kindness?"

"Isn't that
just a parent's heart?"

"How could you not
see your youngest daughter—
one last time?"

"A child
you would have protected
even with your eyes."

"Go now."

"Steady yourself."

"After the harvest—
come again."

"...Yes."

The man fell to his knees.

He bowed.

Deeply.

Then—

he broke down again.

Mother placed a hand
on his shoulder.

Softly—

chanting.

Only then—

my mother,

and Byeongha's father—

began to look like

truly great people.

People to follow.

In that moment—

my mother

became someone

I could not reach.

Not even imagine reaching.

This is a story

I've never found easy

to speak aloud.

chapters.title: Scene 4 - Madam Kitchen (Bueokdaegi)
chapters.content:
Across the road
from my house,

there was a motorcycle shop.

It didn't sell many bikes.

Mostly—

repairs.

It was run
by a young man
in his early twenties.

Jinsung hyung.

One day—

I woke up from a nap.

The house felt...

busy.

Restless.

So I asked Seonju.

"Did something happen?"

"Someone came last night."

"Who?"

"Not family..."

"I don't know."


That evening,

my parents were talking
in low voices.

"Let her stay
for a few days."

"...Alright."

I asked what was going on.

My mother waited
until my father left.

Then—

she spoke.

"I was shocked."

"A grown woman
ran in—"

"completely naked."

"I couldn't
tell her to leave."


What Happened

Jinsung hyung
had been spending time

with youths
from nearby villages.

There was a girl
who liked him.

She said
she would marry him.

Her family said—

"Then you are no longer
our daughter."

"If you leave—
take nothing."

They meant it.

She left
with nothing.

Not even
underwear.

She went
to his house.

But—

it was locked.

He was away.

So she ran—

into our house.

My father said,

"Young men..."

"How do you stop blood
that's already boiling?"

Two days later—

they left together.

Started a life
of their own.

After

I said to Seonju,

"She's braver than you."

"I'm brave too."

"Would you have come
to me like that?"

"...Maybe."

"You know what I'd do
if you went to another man."

"I know."

"You've learned
some bad things."

"Then whose wife
am I?"

"...Alright."

"I lose."

She smiled.

Satisfied.

Madam Kitchen

"Bueokdaegi."

That was the name
of the second child
in that household.

After giving birth
to her first—

she became pregnant again
within a month.

When the time came,

she was resting
at home.

Then suddenly—

something felt wrong.

She sat down—

in the kitchen—

on a chamber pot.

And the baby—

came out.

Just like that.

My mother went over.

Cut the cord.

Helped deliver the child.

After that—

people called the baby,

"Bueokdaegi."

The kitchen child.

In those days,

women weren't always
called by their names.

They were called
by places.

By roles.

By where they came from.

I realized then—

why men
were drawn

to women
with wide hips
and full breasts.

It wasn't just desire.

It was instinct.

Recognizing someone—

who could carry life.

Who could hold
a household together.

After

Mother and Seonju
often looked after the baby.

They would smile—

and call her,

"Bueokdaegi."

chapters.title: Scene 5 - Two, Two, Two Babies
chapters.content:
I heard about Huldra's birth
in my office.

Suddenly—

BANG!

Agent M
and the Messenger

burst in
like the place was on fire.

"Sir! Big trouble!"

I didn't look up.

"Why is it always
big trouble?"

"What is it
this time?"

The Messenger
raised two fingers.

"Two—"

"Two people?"

He shook his head.

"Two—"

"Twelve?"

I laughed.

"Come on.
That's not even a meeting."

Agent M leaned in.

"Two—"

"Twenty?"

I waved my hand.

"Relax.
We'll manage."

I was already
back to my paperwork—

when suddenly—

"NO!!"

"Two."

...

"Hundred."

I froze.

Slowly—

very slowly—

I put my pen down.

"...Oh."

Dead silence.

I leaned back.

"That's not a problem."

A beat.

"That's a budget crisis."

Agent M swallowed.

I rubbed my forehead.

"Well then."

"Looks like
the Dokkaebi..."

"...needs to start
making real money."

A beat.

Then—

we all burst out laughing.

"Was the red ginseng buff
a bit too strong?"

No emergency meeting.

No action plan.

Just laughter—

echoing
through the office.

That day,

we officially decided—

not to count the children,

not to panic
about the forest,

and definitely—

not to touch
the red ginseng again.

At least—

for a while.

chapters.title: Scene 6 - Canvas Theater
chapters.content:
Every year,
in late summer—

Sirak hyung
and the neighborhood kids

started moving together.

I wondered
what they were doing.

They were selling
"invitations."

I don't remember the price—

but it was expensive
for a child.

If you passed
Hari Church,

there was a bridge
toward Georogi.

Under the bridge—

the stream
had dried up.

Only dirt.

Weeds.

They built it there.

A tent.

A projector.

They called it—

a cinema.

Near the entrance,

old movie posters
were taped up.

Layer
on top of layer.

"I heard this one's good."

People said that,

waiting
for the opening day.

The tent was made
of black cloth.

Two—
three layers thick.

No light
could get in.

Kids circled around,

looking—

for a way in.

A hole.

A gap.

Anything.

I didn't care much
about things like that.

But Jia nuna—

my older sister—

went.

With her friends.

She saw a few films.

The next day,

she wanted to go again.

She asked our mother
for money.

The answer—

no.

Then—

she used
the magic word.

"Dong-gi
has never seen a movie."

"He wants to go too."

"He's just not going
because it's dangerous."

"If I take him
with Seonae—"

"We'll just go
and come back."

"It's not for me."

"It's for him."

Mother knew.

Still—

she said,

"Alright."

"If it's the three of you—
this should be enough."

"Seonae—
watch him carefully."

Money changed hands.

I was taken—

like a hostage.


Still—

they found a good spot.

A flat stone.

They sat me down—

and started watching.

That day's film—

Taegkwon-V.

A turtle ship—

flying
through space.

By the time it started,

people had gathered.

From other neighborhoods.

A couple—

leaning
against each other.

The smell—

snacks from home.

Warm.

My mouth watered.

Sometimes—

the film snapped.

Stopped.

People murmured.

The owner ran—

changing reels.

Then—

it started again.

That's how we watched it.

The movie.

The people.

The moment.

And went home—

carrying
memories.

Someday—

I thought—

I should go
to Europe too.

chapters.title: Scene 7 - Manners Maketh a Woman
chapters.content:
When I stepped inside—

Seonju
was already sulking.

Her lips—

stretched out
in a full pout.

"So it's more fun
without me?"

"I'm worse than
an empty barley sack—
just lying there."

"You call yourself my husband,
and you go off alone
to watch something fun?"

"I'll go tomorrow."

"Alone."

She stuck out her tongue.

"Meh—roooong."

A grown woman—

like a child.

I just stood there.

So this—

this was
what people meant by

"bagaji."

Nagging
without sense.

Just then—

Mother's voice.

"Hey—
come out here. Now."

Seonju froze.

Then ran.

"I sent you
with your sister-in-law—"

"to build some bond."

"And this is
how you treat your husband?"

"Did he tell you to go first?"

"Did he say
he wanted to watch it?"

"People say you're pretty—"

"and now you think
you can't do wrong?"

When Mother started—

she didn't stop.

No one stepped in.

I nudged Seonju.

"Hurry—
say you're sorry."

Only then—

"Mother...
I was wrong."

"I didn't think
of your intention."

"I didn't think
of my husband."

"I was wrong."

Mother threw
the basket of corn—

onto the floor.

And went inside.

Seonju stood there.

Then—

quietly—

she picked up
each ear of corn.

Brushed off the dirt.

Placed them back.

One by one.

She went inside.

"Mother...
I was truly wrong."

"We'll eat this
gratefully."

Two days later—

Mother called her again.

"In this house—"

"whether man or woman—"

"the one who carries responsibility..."

"no matter how wrong they are—"

"...is not spoken to carelessly."

"That's our way."

"If someone isn't treated properly at home—"

"they'll be looked down on outside."

"And then—
who feeds this family?"

"Think about that first."

She handed over—

two videotapes.

"They said
these are worth watching."

That evening—

after dinner—

we watched.

The first film—

My Fair Lady.

Seonju watched—

quiet at first.

Then—

her eyes changed.

"Husband—"

"Did you watch
movies like this often?"

"Sometimes."

"In Seoul."

"Places like
Dansungsa."

"Daehan Theater."

"Really?"

"Then which was best?"

"This one."

"And Audrey Hepburn."

"She's the most beautiful woman
in the world."

Seonju blinked.

"Then why don't you live
with Audrey Hepburn?"

"Why me?"

I laughed.

"She's beautiful
on screen."

"But—"

"who could compare
to the woman sitting next to me?"

"Come on—
let me see your face again."

She turned away.

"Tch."

"So you do know
what pretty is."

I slid in
the second tape.

The Bourne Identity.

Gunfire.

Movement.

A man—

who didn't know
who he was.

But still—

he moved.

Like he knew.

Seonju whispered—

"Wow..."

I said nothing.

That night—

something changed.


Epilogue — Seonju's Diary

Today—

many strange things happened.

When I heard
he went without me—

something rose.

So I spoke.

Then—

Mother called.

And I knew.

"I was wrong."

That evening—

two tapes.

And one sentence—

"Manners
Maketh
a Woman."

The first film—

a woman learning—

how to speak,

how to stand,

how to become.

Watching her—

I saw

how small
my world had been.

The kitchen.

The yard.

That was all.

The second film—

a man moving—

without knowing who he was.

Still—

forward.

My husband—

was watching something else.

Not the scene.

The direction.

That look—

felt like

a path.

From that day—

I decided—

I would not remain
in the kitchen
and the yard.

I would see more.

Learn more.

Become more.

Even now—

I can still hear it—

softly—

"Lovely..."

chapters.title: Scene 8 - Autumn Sports Day
chapters.content:
When autumn came—

around September—

the boys practiced
chajeon-nori.

Wooden carts.
Pushing. Colliding.

Mock cavalry games.

The girls—

fan dances,

sogo drums,

running races,

tug-of-war,

ojaemi tossing.

At that age—

moving

was more fun
than studying.

Everything felt
like play.

On the morning
of Sports Day—

flags lined the field.

International flags—

fluttering
in the wind.

A tent—

for the principal,

teachers,

parents,

mothers.

Near the gate—

vendors.

Toys.

Snacks.

Things
we had never seen.

We couldn't look away.

The principal spoke.

Then—

each grade marched.

The band followed.

Pride.

Then the games—

ojaemi,

rolling balls.

The fan dance.

The drum dance.

Parents watched—

quietly.

Something
filling their chests.

Up to that point—

everything
was gentle.

Then—

chajeon-nori.

Heavy.

The boys underneath—

"It's heavy...
heavy..."

Still—

they pushed.

Blue team.

White team.

Manki.

Seok-hyung.

Gigap.

Names—

shouted
into the field.


In the afternoon—

races.

Sprints.

Relays.

We didn't care much
about ours.

We had seen them
too many times.

But—

the adults' games—

were different.

Tug-of-war.

Not a game.

A battlefield.

"Heave—ho!"

"Left—right!"

Bodies moving
as one.


Forearms—

tight.

Strained.

I couldn't
look away.

The mixed relay—

was everything.

Adults and students—

together.

A father.

A mother.

A brother.

A sister.

Passing the baton.

Running—

like something
was chasing them.

"Wooooah—!"

The field roared.

If the baton dropped—

a gasp.

If they caught up—

no one breathed.

By the end—

blue stamps
on our arms.

Notebooks.

Pencils.

Rewards.

Nearby—

makgeolli.

Shaken.

Poured.

Then—

as if waiting—

drums.

Jing.

Kkwaenggwari.

"Jing~~~~"

"Kkae-gaeng kkae-gaeng—"

Bodies moved.

I loved that.

It became a feast.

Watching the adults—

I realized—

they had been
holding it in.

All that time.

Work.

Labor.

Responsibility.

And today—

they let it out.

Someday—

we would be
like them.

Building lives.

And missing this.

But—

something felt off.

During military rule—

events like this
were used.

During colonial times—

games were used.

Control.

And yet—

people still laughed.

Still ran.

Still moved
together.

Maybe—

that was what
kept this place alive.

My mother—

head of
the parents' association.

Six years.

Preparing snacks.

Drinks.

Handling money.

Always—

at the beginning.

At the end.

Busy.

That's when
I learned—

whenever people gather—

someone

must do the work
no one sees.

Like oil—

keeping everything
moving.

That night—

my mother
and my wife—

sat together.

Counting.

Writing.

They didn't look at me.

Not once.

And I—

liked watching
my wife

change.

Little by little.

chapters.title: Scene 9 - Forbidden Love
chapters.content:
After Autumn Sports Day,

the ghosts

started acting strange.

Smiling more.

Softer voices.

Almost—

modern.

***** Text below is optional.*****



Something felt wrong.

So I called Agent M.

"What's going on
in the ghost community?"

"Love is in the air, sir."

"...What?"

"They had Sports Day."

"Since when
do ghosts have Sports Day?"

"Tug-of-war—
eye contact."

"Relay races—
hands brushing."

"Makgeolli—
shared from the same bowl."

A pause.

"Kissing happened."

I sighed.

BANG!

The Messenger burst in.

"Sir!
Serious situation!"

"It's always serious.
What now?"

"The Grim Reaper
has stopped working."

"...Stopped?"

"He fell in love."

"...With?"

"A water ghost."

"They met
during Sports Day."

Silence.

"King Yeomra
ordered immediate arrest."

I leaned back.

"Hold on."

"They can't be together anyway."

"Why not?"

"Why not?"

"The Grim Reaper
is a prosecutor."

"The water ghost—
an illegal resident."

"He's supposed
to arrest her."

The Messenger froze.

"...!!!"

Agent M spoke.

"They're in love, sir."

"Isn't there
another way?"

I thought.

"Isn't the underworld
overloaded these days?"

"Yes!"

"Overnight shifts—
every day!"

I nodded.

"Good."

"Tell her
to turn herself in."

"...Voluntarily?"

"Of course."

"Voluntary surrender—
reduced sentence."

The Messenger lit up.

"Assign her
to assist him."

"Rehabilitation
through labor."

"And after?"

I checked my notes.

"A hundred years."

A pause.

"After a hundred years
working together—"

"they'll be bonded."

"She learns the system."

"Like a private
becoming NCO."

Another beat.

"She becomes
a Grim Reaper."

"Then—"

"they can marry."

"Legally."

Silence.

"She's coming anyway."

"Better to surrender early."

"Lighter sentence."

"Stay in love."

Agent M stood.

"I think
I'll leave early today."

"Where?"

"To deliver
the good news."

I smiled.

"Love is powerful."

"Sometimes—"

"it's the only thing
that dissolves..."

"han."

I paused.

"We may see—"

"a sharp rise
in voluntary confessions."

Epilogue

After that—

voluntary surrenders
increased.

Dramatically.

The workload
stabilized.

Romance—

turned out to be
very effective policy.

chapters.title: Scene 10 - Song of Winter
chapters.content:
About fifty meters upstream
from the wash place—

Cheondangbo.

A small weir.

In summer—
it held water.

In winter—

it became ice.

Wide.

Long.

In the morning—

the sound came first.

jjajak—

jjajajak—

kunk.

It echoed
through the valley.

Along the bank—

dark earth.

Wet.

Only roots remained.

Dry stems—

from last autumn.

One morning—

after breakfast—

I picked up my sled.

And went.

"Dong-gi!"

Jinsung hyung.

From across the road.

I stopped.

He looked
at my sled.

"Hey—
lend me that runner."

He pulled it apart.

The iron spikes—

out.

A thick nail—

driven in.

Hammered.

Then—

ground.

Sharper.

Into the fire—

until it glowed.

Then—

into the snow.

chiiii—

Steam rose.

Steel hardened.

I watched.

And thought—

maybe—

he remembered.

On the ice—

I pushed.

Something was different.

Lighter.

Cleaner.

Each bite—

click.

click.

I moved forward.

Faster.


My wife—

gliding.

Then—

the wind.

Sudden.

Ice dust—

rose.

Hit us
like sand.

Everyone turned.

Waited.

Sometimes—

if you looked down—

you could see

fish.

Moving slowly.

And one leaf—

red.

From last autumn.

Drifting.

That's how we knew.

It was over.

Epilogue

A year later—

before they left
for the city—

Jinsung hyung's family
invited us.

We went.

Together.

Hobbang—

steamed.

Sweet potatoes—

roasted.

Quiet days.

Madam Kitchen—

sitting
with her family.


That—

is what I remember.
